l: Euphaes, Description of Greece
s: Euphaes, king of the Messenians, succeeds his father Antiochus as king of Messenia. After the Lacedæmonians capture Amphea, he urges resistance, trains and commands his people, is mortally wounded fighting Theopompus, dies after thirteen years, and is succeeded by Aristodemus.

l: Amphea, Description of Greece
s: Amphea is a small Messenian town near Laconia on a high, well-watered hill, valuable as a war base. Lacedæmonians capture it by night through open gates, kill those found there, including suppliants, occupy it with a garrison, and later use that garrison to ambush Tisis.

l: capture of Amphea, Description of Greece
s: The capture of Amphea, the first Lacedæmonian attack against Messenia in the second year of the ninth Olympiad, occurs under Alcamenes after the town is found ungarrisoned. Escaped inhabitants report enslavement or suffering, prompting the Messenians to convene at Stenyclerus and prepare urgently for war.

l: Messenian–Lacedæmonian conflict, Description of Greece
s: is_caused_by Polychares [according to the Lacedæmonian account] The conflict arose from competing traditions about the death of Teleclus, the treatment of Polychares and Euæphnus, and earlier disputes involving Cresphontes and the division of territory. The Lacedæmonians rejected arbitration and ultimately began open hostilities with the capture of Amphea.

l: mysteries of the Great Goddesses, Description of Greece
s: are_held_at Andania [still celebrated there] The mysteries of the Great Goddesses were brought from Eleusis to Messenia by Caucon and later reformed or taught by Lycus and Methapus. They were associated with Andania, where they continued to be celebrated, and Sybotas required annual rites before them.

l: Aristomenes, Description of Greece
s: Aristomenes is presented as a Messenian hero, leader, king, and commander in chief in the second battle between the Messenians and Lacedæmonians. Said to be descended from the Æpytidæ and son of Nicomedes, he first brought honor to Messene. After the battle of Deræ, young leaders promoted resistance to Spartan rule and the Messenians elected him king. He fought boldly: he displayed a shield at Athene Chalciœcus, routed Lacedæmonian forces, raided Pharis, escaped Ceadas, defeated Corinthian auxiliaries, and offered Hecatomphonia after killing one hundred enemies. Captured by Cretan bowmen, he was saved by a Messenian maiden. During the siege of Eira, he led raids, rescued a merchant, defended and encouraged the Messenians, and was wounded. Though an oracle had shown him their cause was doomed, he organized the escape of the people after Theoclus died. His later plan to capture Sparta with 500 Messenians failed through Aristocrates' betrayal. He buried Messene's sacred records on Mount Ithome for its future recovery and declined leadership of a new colony. He arranged marriages for his sister Agnagora and two daughters, consulted Delphi, and died of illness at Rhodes while intending to seek vengeance. Damagetus honored him as the noblest Greek of his time and received a monument for him; Messene claimed his tomb. Messenians also said he aided the Thebans at Leuctra, while his shield was displayed there and later returned to Trophonius' temple.

l: Tyrtæus, Description of Greece
s: Tyrtæus is a schoolmaster sent from Athens to Sparta, who composed and recited elegiac verses and anapæsts about the former war; his verses later dated Ithome’s evacuation and described twenty years of the first Messenian War.

l: Dryopes, Description of Greece
s: The Dryopes were neighbours of the Lycoritæ near Mount Parnassus, named for their founder; defeated by Hercules, their descendants settled in the Peloponnese and Styra, while Asinæi retained their name, temples, and mysteries.

l: first Messenian battle, Description of Greece
s: is_fought_between Messenians [and the Lacedæmonians] In the first major battle, Euphaes and the Messenians meet the Lacedæmonians at a place protected by a deep ravine. Euphaes’s men fortify their camp, while the fighting ends without a decisive victory and both sides later bury their dead.

l: second battle between the Messenians and Lacedæmonians, Description of Greece
s: ends_in death of Euphaes [after he received many mortal wounds] The second battle is fought after both Lacedæmonian kings lead an army against the Messenians. Euphaes’s division routs Theopompus’s troops, Pytharatus is killed on the Messenian side, and Euphaes is mortally wounded before the battle ends at nightfall.

l: Messenian oracle, Description of Greece
s: requires sacrifice of a pure virgin [by night to the gods below] The oracle brought from Delphi commands the Messenians to sacrifice a pure virgin from the family of the Æpytidæ by night. If no suitable Æpytidæ could be found, the oracle allowed a willing volunteer from another family.

l: sacrifice of a pure virgin, Description of Greece
s: is_selected_from Æpytidæ [by lot] The Æpytidæ draw lots, but the selected daughter of Lyciscus is rejected when Epebolus reveals that she is not truly Lyciscus’s daughter. Aristodemus then kills his own daughter after a false accusation of pregnancy, and Euphaes persuades the Messenians to regard her death as fulfilling the oracle.

l: warfare, Description of Greece
s: is_practised_by Messenians [throughout Euphaes's reign] The warfare involves raids, fortified towns, heavy-armed infantry, cavalry, light-armed troops, and Cretan archers serving the Lacedæmonians. The combatants show intense courage, ask no quarter, and generally avoid pursuing fleeing enemies too far or breaking their formations.

l: Phyleus, Description of Greece
s: Phyleus, eldest son of Augeas, is expelled for defending just reward for Hercules, receives Elis and captives, settles its affairs, then returns to Dulichium.

l: Deræ, Description of Greece
s: Deræ was a place in Messenia where the Messenians and Lacedæmonians fought during the first year of the second Messenian War. Neither side had allies, and the battle was undecided.

l: the second war between the Lacedæmonians and the Messenians, Description of Greece
s: The second war between the Messenians and Lacedæmonians began thirty-nine years after Ithome’s capture, when Messenian Helots revolted after suppliants were killed at Tænarum. The rebels occupied Ithome, fought an undecided battle at Deræ, and assembled allies for Boar’s Memorial, while the Lacedæmonians sought allied aid. It ended with Eira’s capture in the first year of the 28th Olympiad.

l: battle of Deræ, Description of Greece
s: The battle of Deræ, fought without allies in the first year of the second Messenian War, ended undecided; afterward the Messenians elected Aristomenes king and commander in chief.

l: battle at Boar’s Memorial, Description of Greece
s: The battle at Boar’s Memorial was prepared one year after the battle of Deræ, when both sides had assembled allies. The Messenians had support from Elis, Arcadia, Argos, Sicyon, the priests from Eleusis, and the descendants of Androcles, while the Lacedæmonians were supported by the Corinthians and some people of Lepreum; the Asinæi remained neutral.

l: capture and evacuation of Ithome, Description of Greece
s: The Messenians evacuated Ithome after holding it for about five months under siege and after twenty full years of war. The Lacedæmonians then captured the other Messenian cities and first razed Ithome to the ground.

l: tripods of Zeus of Ithome, Description of Greece
s: is_a votive offerings [made of clay or wood in the contest over the oracle] A Delphic oracle promised the Messenian land to those who first set up one hundred tripods at the altar of Zeus of Ithome. The Messenians prepared wooden tripods, while Œbalus secretly placed one hundred clay tripods there for Sparta; the Messenians then placed their wooden tripods at the altar as well.

l: Theoclus the seer, Description of Greece
s: Theoclus is a Messenian seer descended from Eumantis and father of Manticlus. After consulting Delphi with Aristomenes, he interprets the Pythian oracle and signs in nature as foretelling Messene's end, warns Aristomenes, and nevertheless helps defend Eira. He encourages the Messenians, fights the Lacedæmonians, kills several, and dies of wounds during Eira's capture.

l: Aristocrates, Description of Greece
s: Aristocrates, son of Icetas, is king and general of the Arcadians and native of Trapezus. Bribed by the Lacedæmonians, he refuses to aid the Messenians, orders the Arcadians to flee at the Great Trench, and abandons the Messenian forces. He later reveals the plan of 500 Messenian volunteers to Anaxander. Exposed as a traitor, he is stoned by the Arcadians and cast beyond their borders.

l: Gorgus the son of Aristomenes, Description of Greece
s: Gorgus, son of Aristomenes, was a uniquely four-time Olympic pentathlon victor who also won the double course and heavy-armour race. He defended Eira, led retreating Messenians, women, and children, and later led their Sicilian settlement.

l: Emperamus, Description of Greece
s: leads Emperamus and the Spartans [during the assault on Eira] Emperamus led the Spartan force through the darkness and rain to Eira, where they entered the citadel by scaling its walls. He was pleased when Aristomenes signaled that the Messenians wished to withdraw, and he allowed them to pass through the lines.

l: Eira, Description of Greece
s: Eira is a mountain stronghold and refuge of the Messenians after defeat at the Great Trench. Besieged by the Lacedæmonians for eleven years, it is defended despite improvised fortifications and raids. During a violent rainstorm, abandoned guards and a herdsman's disclosure enable Emperamus and the Spartan force to scale its citadel. Its capture ends the second war; inhabitants become Helots.

l: Mount Lycæus, Description of Greece
s: is_a place of refuge [for the surviving Messenians] Mount Lycæus was where the Arcadians met and welcomed the surviving Messenians after the fall of Eira. Aristomenes planned his attack on Sparta there, and Aristocrates’ betrayal was exposed before the Arcadians.

l: Ceadas, Description of Greece
s: is_a underground cavern [used by the Lacedæmonians for condemned malefactors] Ceadas is the underground cavern into which the Lacedæmonians throw their greatest malefactors. Aristomenes and captured Messenian soldiers are cast into it, but Aristomenes survives, follows a fox to an opening, enlarges the passage, and escapes.

l: siege of Eira, Description of Greece
s: lasts eleven years [after the disaster at the Great Trench] The siege of Eira lasts eleven years after the Messenian defeat at the Great Trench. During it, the Messenians conduct raids, while the Lacedæmonians attempt to take the stronghold and receive assistance from Corinthian troops and Cretan bowmen. The siege approaches its conclusion when a deserter informs Emperamus how the abandoned guard posts can be exploited.

l: fall of Eira, Description of Greece
s: is_foretold_by oracle of the Pythian Priestess concerning Messene [through the sign of the he-goat drinking from the Neda] The fall of Eira is foretold by the oracle concerning the he-goat drinking from the Neda and is brought nearer when a herdsman learns that the Messenian guards have left their posts during heavy rain. The herdsman deserts to the Lacedæmonians and tells Emperamus how the stronghold can be captured.

l: Messenian resistance at Eira, Description of Greece
s: lasts eleven years [after the disaster at the Great Trench] The Messenian resistance at Eira continues for eleven years after the disaster at the Great Trench. Aristomenes leads raids against Laconia and the Messenians ransom captives and property, while the defenders withstand the Lacedæmonian blockade. The resistance is undermined when a storm causes the guards to leave their posts and a herdsman betrays the stronghold's vulnerability.

l: Manticlus, Description of Greece
s: Manticlus, a Messenian leader, fought among Eira’s first defenders, led retreating Messenians with Gorgus, urged sailing to Sardinia, led settlement in Sicily, and built Hercules’ temple.

l: Emperamus and the Spartans, Description of Greece
s: is_a Spartan force They marched through darkness and heavy rain, entered Eira by scaling its walls, and fought the Messenians. They allowed Aristomenes and the retreating Messenians to pass through their lines rather than provoke men who were desperate and enraged.

l: the capture of Eira, Description of Greece
s: ends the second war between the Lacedæmonians and the Messenians The capture of Eira followed three days and nights of continuous fighting in severe rain and cold. It caused the fall of the last Messenian stronghold, the enslavement of many Messenians as Helots, and the flight of the remaining exiles.

l: the 500 Messenian volunteers, Description of Greece
s: is_a Messenian volunteers [selected by Aristomenes for a desperate undertaking] Aristomenes selected 500 Messenians known to be willing to risk their lives and asked whether they would die with him to avenge their country. They agreed to his plan to attack Sparta, but the plan was revealed to the Lacedæmonians before it could be carried out.

l: the betrayal of Aristocrates, Description of Greece
s: is_exposed_by the Arcadian slave Aristocrates betrayed Aristomenes by sending Anaxander a letter revealing the planned attack on Sparta. The letter was intercepted by Arcadians, who showed Anaxander’s reply to the people and thereby exposed Aristocrates as a traitor.

l: Cyllene, Description of Greece
s: Cyllene is the arsenal and dockyard of Elis, about 120 stades away, with a fine harbor facing Sicily and temples of Æsculapius and Aphrodite. After Eira fell, maritime people and exiled Messenians took refuge there, wintered with Elis’s support, and planned a new home.

l: the Messenian colony, Description of Greece
s: is_founded_at Messene [in Sicily, after the conquest of Zancle] The Messenian colony was established in Sicily after the exiles accepted Anaxilas’ invitation and conquered Zancle. Its people changed the town’s name to Messene, and Manticlus built a temple of Hercules there.

l: Anaxilas, Description of Greece
s: Anaxilas, king of Rhegium and fourth in descent from Alcidamidas, invited Messenian exiles to seize Zancle, aided its conquest by sea blockade, and urged killing suppliants and enslaving others.

l: Zancle, Description of Greece
s: Zancle, a fortified pirate base in fertile Sicily, was conquered by Anaxilas and the Messenians; its people were spared, incorporated, and the place renamed Messene.

l: the people of Zancle, Description of Greece
s: The people of Zancle are defeated by Anaxilas at sea and Messenians on land, lose their fort, seek sanctuary, and, spared from death or enslavement, unite with the Messenian colony.

l: Diagorid family, Description of Greece
s: The Diagorid family included Diagoras, his sons Acusilaus, Damagetus, and Dorieus, and his descendants Eucles and Pisirodus. Its members achieved numerous victories at Olympia and other games, and statues of the family were displayed together at Olympia.

l: Diagoras, Description of Greece
s: Diagoras was a Rhodian boxer and head of the Diagorid family. He won Olympic boxing among men, had a statue by Callicles at Olympia, and, after his sons Acusilaus and Damagetus won, was carried on their shoulders.

l: Epiteles, Description of Greece
s: Epiteles, an Argive general and restorer of Messene, is directed in a dream to dig at Ithome, where he finds a brass urn containing written Mysteries and brings it to Epaminondas.

l: Messene (city), Description of Greece
s: is_a capital of Messenia [rebuilt after the return of the Messenians] The restored Messenians built Messene as a new capital after Epaminondas selected its site and received favorable omens. They constructed its walls, houses, streets, and temples, and also restored other Messenian towns.

l: Naupactus, Description of Greece
s: The Athenians gave Naupactus to the Messenians who surrendered at Ithome after taking it from the Locrians called Ozolæ. Naupactus became a Messenian base against the Peloponnese, and after its loss the Messenians dispersed to Sicily and Libya.

l: Œniadæ, Description of Greece
s: The Messenians attacked Œniadæ, defeated its inhabitants, and occupied the town for about a year. The Acarnanians later besieged it, and the Messenians escaped by night after their supplies were exhausted, fighting their way through to Naupactus.

l: Messenian return to the Peloponnese, Description of Greece
s: The Messenian return to the Peloponnese followed the Theban victory at Leuctra and the recall issued by the Thebans. The exiles returned with strong attachment to their homeland and hatred of the Lacedæmonians, rebuilt Messene and other towns, and preserved their national customs and Doric dialect.

l: siege of Œniadæ, Description of Greece
s: During the siege of Œniadæ, the Messenians initially defeated or repelled Acarnanian attacks but were eventually blockaded until their provisions ran out in the eighth month. They then escaped by night, losing about 300 men but killing more Acarnanians, and reached Naupactus with help from the Ætolians.

l: Messenian Mysteries, Description of Greece
s: rank second only to Eleusinian Mysteries [in sanctity, in Pausanias’ opinion] The Messenian Mysteries were recovered at Ithome when Epiteles found a brass urn containing their written records. The priests entered the records in books, and they sacrificed to the Great Goddesses and Caucon during the restoration of Messene.

l: restoration of Messene, Description of Greece
s: The restoration of Messene was the Messenian return to their ancestral country after dispersion. After the victory at Leuctra, Epaminondas, Epiteles, the Thebans, and allies examined the site through omens, sacrificed to gods and heroes, and built the city and restored other towns. Later the Messenians faced conflicts, aided Arcadians, captured Sparta, and rejoined the Achæan League.

l: Demetrius, son of Philip, Description of Greece
s: Demetrius, son of Philip, was a Macedonian commander who led Philip's force to the Peloponnese for money, secretly entered Messene, and was defeated by its defenders.

l: Philopœmen, son of Craugis, Description of Greece
s: Philopœmen, son of Craugis, escaped Megalopolis with surviving Arcadians and was received by Messenians; he later attacked Nabis by night, then was captured and killed during conflict with Messenians.

l: Dinocrates, Description of Greece
s: Dinocrates, a prominent Messenian newly elected ruler, forced Lycortas and the Achæan army from Messenia, then occupied routes toward Arcadia to protect Messenians and neighboring districts.

l: Abia, Description of Greece
s: Abia is a town by the sea in Messenia, once called Ire; tradition says Abia, nurse of Glenus, built a temple of Hercules and gave it her name.

l: Thuria, Description of Greece
s: Thuria, said to be Homer’s Anthea, was given by Augustus to the Spartans; its inhabitants moved from an ancient height to the plain by the Aris, leaving ruins and a Syrian goddess’s temple above.

l: Pamisus, Description of Greece
s: The Pamisus is a clear, limpid river in Messenia, flowing through arable land for about 10 stades to the sea; spring fish swim upstream, and Corone stands on its right bank near its mouth.

l: Clepsydra, Description of Greece
s: Clepsydra is a spring and well beneath Mount Ithome near Ithome’s gates, supplying Zeus’s temple and the Arsinoe conduit; Messenians said Ithome and Neda washed infant Zeus there.

l: Carnasian grove, Description of Greece
s: Carnasian grove, formerly called Œchalia, stood opposite the plain of Stenyclerus, mostly of cypresses. It contained statues of Carnean Apollo, Hermes, and the Virgin, and the unrevealed Messenian Mysteries.

l: capture of Messene, Description of Greece
s: involved Demetrius, son of Philip [Macedonian attack] The attempted capture of Messene occurred when Demetrius, son of Philip, led Macedonian troops into the town before dawn. The inhabitants first mistook them for Lacedæmonians, then attacked them after recognizing their Macedonian arms and language; the Macedonians were defeated and many died among the rocks of Ithome.

l: Corone, Description of Greece
s: Corone is a coastal town under Mathia, 80 stades from the Pamisus and 40 from Colonides. Formerly called Æpea, it was renamed Coronea after the restoration of the Messenians and later called Corone. It has temples of Artemis, Dionysus, and Æsculapius, and brazen statues of Zeus Soter and Athene.

l: Illyrians, Description of Greece
s: capture Mothone's capture by the Illyrians [by deception and piracy] The Illyrians became masters of Epirus by a sudden attack and later equipped a fleet for piratic raids. At Mothone they pretended to trade peacefully, then captured many men and even more women and sailed away with them.

l: Coryphasium, Description of Greece
s: is_a promontory [near Pylos] The promontory of Coryphasium is about 100 stades from Mothone. Pylos lies near it.

l: Mothone's capture by the Illyrians, Description of Greece
s: is_a piratic attack [the town was partly depopulated] The Illyrians first anchored at Mothone as if they intended friendly commerce and gradually encouraged the inhabitants to come aboard their ships. When the traffic had grown, they seized many men and more women, put them on board, and sailed away toward the Ionian sea, leaving the town partly stripped of its population.

l: Ætolus, Description of Greece
s: Ætolus succeeds Epeus, accidentally kills Apis during funeral games, flees to the Achelous region, and gives Ætolia its name.

l: Œnomaus, Description of Greece
s: Œnomaus is a helmeted figure on the Olympia temple gable, beside his wife Sterope, with charioteer Myrtilus, two grooms, a chariot, and four horses.

l: Eleus, Description of Greece
s: Eleus, son of Eurycyde and allegedly Poseidon, ruled the Epeans, who became known as Eleans during his reign.

l: Pisa, Description of Greece
s: Pisa, founded by Pisus, first assists Elis against Hercules. It controls territory near Olympia, then loses it to Elis and repeatedly contests the Olympic games, joining neighboring communities. After conflict over control of the games, Elis defeats and razes Pisa and its supporting towns.

l: Oxylus, Description of Greece
s: Oxylus, an Ætolian who had fled after accidentally killing his brother, led the Dorians to the Peloponnese and received the kingdom of Elis. He defeated Elis’s champion through a single combat, allowed the Epeans to remain, introduced Ætolian colonists, consolidated the population of Elis, and invited Agorius and other Achæans to settle there.

l: Olympic truce, Description of Greece
s: Iphitus established a truce that lasted as long as the games at Olympia continued. The truce formed part of his restoration of the Olympian games.

l: Temple of Zeus at Olympia, Description of Greece
s: The Temple of Zeus at Olympia is a Doric stone building designed by Libon of Elis, 68 feet high, 95 feet wide, and 230 feet long. Its Pentelican marble-tile roof and gables show the chariot race between Pelops and Œnomaus and the Lapithæ-Centaurs fight. It contains a gold-and-ivory statue, veil, offerings, statues, crowns, shields, pillars, and dedications.

l: people of Elis, Description of Greece
s: The people of Elis are a group defined by recurring religious practice: monthly sacrifices with specified offerings, libations to several gods and heroes, votive dedications, and preserved oracle consultations. They have a citadel at Elis and honor Dionysus most of all, celebrating the Thyia, during which they report wine miraculously appearing in sealed flagons.

l: Samicum, Description of Greece
s: Samicum was a coastal place near the district of Triphylia and the city of Lepreus. A road from Samicum led to Lepreus beside the river Aniger, and the river had its outlet to the sea after passing through Samicum. Samia, a town above Samicum, was said to have been made into an offensive fortress against the Arcadians by Polysperchon.

l: Lepreus, Description of Greece
s: Lepreus was a city in Triphylia, long subject to Elis though its people claimed Arcadian belonging. Its name was variously linked to Lepreus or Leprea, children of Pyrgeus, or early leprosy. It had a spring and, later, a temple of Demeter amid remembered lost shrines and tombs.

l: Aniger, Description of Greece
s: Aniger is a river rising in the Arcadian mountain Lapithus and flowing to the sea near Samicum. Its wind-blocked, foul-smelling waters were fishless before receiving Acidas and yielded inedible fish afterward. Traditions explained the smell through washed wounds, poison, or purifications; nearby, leprosy sufferers prayed, sacrificed, and bathed at its Nymphs’ cave for healing.

l: Scillus, Description of Greece
s: Scillus, a town in Triphylia, allied with Pisa against Elis; Elis dispossessed its inhabitants, then the Lacedæmonians took it and gave it to Xenophon. Its district had hunting animals and the river Selinus.

l: Pisirodus, Description of Greece
s: Pisirodus, son of Callipatira and grandson of Diagoras, won the Olympic boys’ boxing prize; after his mother brought him disguised as a trainer, he received a statue near his maternal grandfather’s at Altis.

l: Olympian contests, Description of Greece
s: Olympian contests are instituted by Idæan Hercules, who gives them their name. Women of Elis who compete or cross the Alpheus on forbidden days face being hurled from Mount Typæum; Callipatira is spared after disguising herself for her son, and athletes are required to compete naked. Hiero, Aratus, and Agesarchus are later commemorated as victors.

l: pancratium, Description of Greece
s: The pancratium was an Olympic athletic contest combining boxing and wrestling. Introduced at Olympia in the eighth Olympiad after the 25th, it was initially scheduled after horse-races before the programme changed. A boys' event was added in the 145th Olympiad. Lygdamis, Phædimus, Polydamas, Artemidorus, Clitomachus, Caprus, and others won or contested it.

l: Umpires of Elis, Description of Greece
s: Umpires of Elis began with Iphitus alone, followed by the posterity of Oxylus. Their number changed with Elis’s organization and tribes: two, nine, ten, twelve, eight after territory loss, and finally ten. They swore over a boar’s entrails to judge honestly without bribes.

l: Altis, Description of Greece
s: Altis is the sacred grove of Zeus at Olympia, also a sanctuary precinct and Olympic sanctuary. Its name is described as a slightly altered form of the Greek word for grove, and Pindar used it in an ode for a victor at Olympia. It is above all a densely furnished sacred and ceremonial place: it has a processional road and entrance, numerous altars, temples, city treasuries, the Town Hall of the people of Elis, the Hippodamium, and facilities associated with the Olympian games. Its altars belong to many named gods and figures, while its temples include the Temple of the Mother. Throughout it stand statues, pillars, monuments, and votive offerings from athletes, communities, and individuals, including statues of Olympic victors, statues of Zeus made from athletic fines, the largest brazen Zeus, and the pillar of Oenomaus. Particular objects include Phormis’s bronze horse, the Mendæan offerings, and a brazen trophy beneath plane-trees, dedicated by the people of Elis from Lacedæmonian spoils. Altis also preserves conflict: during the Lacedæmonian invasion, the people of Elis defended themselves from its temples and high buildings, and later a trophy marked victory over the Laconians. Its described course moves through entrances, altars, temples, walls, monuments, and game-related places, ending with its many statues, offerings, treasuries, and facilities.

l: statue of Zeus, Description of Greece
s: The statue of Zeus at Olympia was made by Phidias, identified as an Athenian son of Charmides by an inscription at its base, and stood in a decorated temple.

l: chariot race between Pelops and Œnomaus, Description of Greece
s: is_depicted_on temple of Zeus at Olympia [in bas relief on the gable] The chariot race between Pelops and Œnomaus was represented in bas relief on one of the temple’s gables at Olympia. The scene showed both chariots in motion, with Zeus in the center and the associated figures, horses, and rivers arranged on either side.

l: Hippodamia, Description of Greece
s: Hippodamia was a woman whose suitors Oinomaus killed before Pelops won a race against him and married her; Pelops later buried the suitors together partly from affection for her. In gratitude for the marriage, she selected sixteen matrons and inaugurated Hera’s games, and they maintained Hippodamia’s dance. After Pelops grew angry over Chrysippus’s death, she fled to Midea; her remains were brought to Olympia, where women performed annual rites at the Hippodamium.

l: Labours of Hercules, Description of Greece
s: The Labours of Hercules are exploits represented in relief at Olympia, including hunting the Erymanthian boar, taking Diomede’s mares and the Amazon’s belt, stealing Geryon’s oxen, supporting Atlas’s load, clearing Elis, and encounters with the stag, Minotaur, birds, hydra, and lion.

l: Zeus statue, Description of Greece
s: Zeus statue is a gold-and-ivory statue depicting Olympian Zeus, seated on a throne in gold robe, sandals, and olive-leaf crown, holding Victory and a jewelled eagle sceptre; at Olympia, its ivory is protected with oil against grove dampness.

l: throne of Zeus, Description of Greece
s: The throne is a richly adorned throne at Olympia, made with gold, precious stones, ebony, ivory, painted animals, and worked figures. Four feet, pillars, Victories, Theban boys, and enclosing panels shape it. Its decoration unfolds through painted panels and divisions showing Hercules, Amazons, and other contests, battles, and figures.

l: enclosure sacred to Pelops, Description of Greece
s: The grove of Pelops, traditionally dedicated by Hercules, lies north of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia. Enclosed, tree-planted, and filled with statues and offerings, it is entered from the west; black-ram sacrifices restrict entry to the temple.

l: altar of Olympian Zeus, Description of Greece
s: is 22 feet high The altar of Olympian Zeus is made from the debris of the thigh bones of sacrificed victims and stands between the grove of Pelops and the Temple of Hera. It has a lower pro-altar and a higher altar, with steps to the former and debris steps to the latter; victims are sacrificed below, while their thigh bones are burned above.

l: Olympian altar ritual, Description of Greece
s: begins_with Vesta [in the order of Elis sacrifices] The altar ritual at Olympia includes sacrifices in a prescribed sequence, beginning with Vesta and continuing with Olympian Zeus, Hermes, Artemis, Athena, Alpheus, and other deities. At the great altar, victims are sacrificed at the lower level and their thigh bones are burned at the top; seers annually renew the altar with debris mixed with water from the Alpheus.

l: Town Hall of the people of Elis, Description of Greece
s: situated_in Altis [near the outlet beyond the gymnasium] The Town Hall stands within Altis near the outlet beyond the gymnasium. It contains a hearth with a continually burning fire, an altar of Pan, and a banqueting-hall where victors at Olympia are entertained.

l: gymnasium of Elis, Description of Greece
s: is_a gymnasium [used for training athletes before Olympia] The gymnasium of Elis is an old training complex where athletes prepare before going to Olympia. It contains the Colonnade, racecourses, the Plethrium for testing athletes, altars and statues, the Square for wrestling, Maltho for the lads, and the Lalichmium council chamber for rhetorical practice and public criticism of writings.

l: temple of Hera, Description of Greece
s: Scillus built this large Doric temple for Hera about eight years after Oxylus became king at Elis; 63 feet long, it contains statues and Cypselus's chest.

l: Hera Festival, Description of Greece
s: presided_over_by sixteen matrons [every fifth year] The Hera Festival includes races for maidens of different ages, with the youngest racing first and the eldest last. Victors receive olive crowns, a portion of the heifer sacrificed to Hera, and painted representations are made for Hera.

l: sixteen matrons, Description of Greece
s: The sixteen matrons, first selected from sixteen cities to arbitrate Elis–Pisa disputes, later chosen two from each of eight tribes, preside over the Hera Festival, weave Hera’s shawl every fifth year, and conduct Physcoa’s and Hippodamia’s dances.

l: chest of Cypselus, Description of Greece
s: The chest of Cypselus is a cedar votive offering decorated with ivory, gold, and carved cedar figures. It bears old Greek inscriptions, including ox-fashion writing, that identify or describe mythic scenes. From Pelops, Pelias, Hercules, and the Harpies, its imagery continues through Death and Sleep, Jason and Medea, Atlas, Achilles, and Memnon; its maker remains uncertain, though Eumelus the Corinthian is suspected.

l: Hera’s maiden race, Description of Greece
s: Hera’s maiden race at Olympia is a maiden race on a course shortened one-sixth of a stade; maidens run hair down in short tunics, and victors receive olive crowns.

l: sacrifices at the altars, Description of Greece
s: A monthly Elis sacrifice: people burn frankincense and honey cakes, decorate altars with olive branches, and pour wine, withholding it from the Nymphs, Mistresses, and joint altar.

l: Eupolus, Description of Greece
s: Eupolus of Thessaly bribed athletes to win boxing at Olympia, was fined by Elis with them, and the penalties funded six statues of Zeus.

l: Caprus of Elis, Description of Greece
s: Caprus of Elis, son of Pythagoras, became the first recorded athlete to win Olympia’s wrestling and pancratium prizes on one day, defeating Pæanius and Clitomachus; two statues honored him there.

l: bribery at Olympia, Description of Greece
s: Bribery at Olympia involved athletes or their associates paying opponents to lose or secure a victory. The unit recounts cases involving Eupolus, Callippus, Eudelus, and the boxers Didas and Sarapammon, as well as Damonicus bribing Sosander on behalf of his son.

l: fines imposed for cheating, Description of Greece
s: Fines imposed on athletes and those responsible for their misconduct were used to create statues of Zeus and other memorials. The unit records fines for bribery, cheating, lateness, and cowardice, including the fines imposed on Eupolus and his opponents, Callippus and his opponents, and later boxers.

l: statues of Zeus, Description of Greece
s: Statues of Zeus at Olympia, located in Altis, vary in size, appearance, attributes, and dedication; they include a young Zeus with a necklace and offerings from many peoples and places.

l: Hippodamium, Description of Greece
s: Hippodamium is a walled, acre-sized enclosure inside Altis, annually entered by women who sacrifice to Hippodamia and perform rites in her honor.

l: Greeks who fought at Platæa, Description of Greece
s: erected Zeus [a statue at Olympia] The Greeks who fought at Platæa against Mardonius and the Medes dedicated a statue of Zeus at Olympia. The states that took part in the action were inscribed on the right side of its basement, beginning with the Lacedæmonians and followed by the Athenians and other participating communities.

l: 30-year peace between Sparta and Athens, Description of Greece
s: The 30-year peace was an agreement between Lacedæmonians and Athenians, made after Athens’ second reduction of Eubœa, excluding Argives but permitting private friendship, and recorded on a brazen pillar near Zeus’ statue.

l: Council Chamber statue of Zeus, Description of Greece
s: Zeus the God of Oaths is the most terrifying statue of Zeus, in the Council Chamber. Holding a thunderbolt in each hand, it receives oaths from athletes, their relatives, trainers, and umpires.

l: Olympic athletes, Description of Greece
s: swear_over oath over the entrails of a boar [not to cheat at the Olympian games] The Olympic athletes swear before Zeus the God of Oaths, over the entrails of a boar, that they will not cheat at the games. They also swear that they have trained carefully for ten months.

l: Messenians at the Sicilian Strait, Description of Greece
s: sent chorus of thirty-five boys [to Rhegium for the national feast] The Messenians at the Sicilian Strait traditionally sent thirty-five boys, a choir-master, and a piper to Rhegium for a national feast. After all of them died in a sea disaster, they placed brazen effigies of the boys, the choir-master, and the piper at Olympia.

l: shipwreck in the Sicilian Strait, Description of Greece
s: A vessel carrying the Messenians’ chorus, choir-master, and piper was wrecked in the Sicilian Strait, and none of those aboard survived. The account attributes the danger to the strait’s winds, meeting seas, strong swell, sea-monsters, and difficulty reaching shore.

l: Sicilian Strait, Description of Greece
s: is_formed_by Sicilian Sea [together with the Tyrrhenian Sea] The Sicilian Strait is described as extremely stormy, where the Sicilian and Tyrrhenian seas meet and where strong ebb and flow creates a tremendous swell even in calm weather. It is also said to contain many sea-monsters and to offer shipwrecked mariners little chance of reaching safety.

l: brazen effigies of the drowned chorus, Description of Greece
s: were_made_by Callon of Elis The brazen effigies of the drowned chorus, its choir-master, and its piper were erected at Olympia by the grieving Messenians at the Sicilian Strait. The effigies were made by Callon of Elis, and Hippias later composed elegiac lines for them.

l: Onatas the Æginetan, Description of Greece
s: Onatas, son of Micon and an Æginetan, made Hercules and Idomeneus among votive offerings at Olympia; an inscription credits him with many works, and he is ranked among the greatest sculptors since Dædalus and the Attic school.

l: Micythus, Description of Greece
s: Micythus was treasurer of Anaxilas and, when Anaxilas was king at Rhegium, his slave. The inscriptions name him son of Chœrus and native of Rhegium, alternatively Messene near the Strait. After Anaxilas’s death he lived at Tegea. At Olympia he placed many votive offerings, fulfilling a vow for his son’s recovery from a wasting consumption: Proserpine, Aphrodite, Ganymede, Artemis, Homer, Hesiod, Æsculapius, Hygiea, and Agon with dumb bells, including works by Argive Glaucus and Dionysius. Nero later removed some offerings.

l: Argive Glaucus, Description of Greece
s: He made several works among Micythus’s offerings at Olympia, including Amphitrite, Poseidon, Vesta, Proserpine, Aphrodite, Ganymede, Artemis, Homer, Hesiod, Æsculapius, and Hygiea. He also made the statue of Athene that stood near the larger offerings of Micythus.

l: Phormis, Description of Greece
s: Phormis was a Mænalian from Mænalus who went to Sicily, served Gelon and then Hiero, showed great valor, and became wealthy. He was honored through offerings at Olympia and Delphi, including images of horses, charioteers, and himself fighting enemies, dedicated by Lycortas.

l: horses and charioteers of Phormis, Description of Greece
s: includes Phormis’s horse [the first horse and groom] Phormis’s offerings at Olympia consisted of two horses and two charioteers, with one charioteer beside each horse. The first horse and groom were made by Dionysius the Argive, and the second by the Æginetan Simo.

l: Phormis’s horse, Description of Greece
s: A brazen horse, made by Dionysius the Argive and dedicated by Phormis, stands on a polished basement with its tail lost. Though smaller and less beautiful than many horses at Olympia, it attracts stallions year-round, provoking mounting attempts stopped only by force or whips.

l: Phormis’s votive offerings, Description of Greece
s: Phormis’s votive offerings at Olympia consisted of two horses, two charioteers, and a fighting image; though Lycortas dedicated the image, Greeks counted it among Phormis’s offerings.

l: votive offerings, Description of Greece
s: include statues of Olympic victors [among the offerings at Olympia] Pausanias's account focuses on votive offerings, especially statues and related monuments dedicated at Olympia. These offerings commemorate athletic victories, rulers, military achievements, and honored individuals.

l: Nemean games, Description of Greece
s: is_a Greek athletic games [held at Nemea] The Nemean games are mentioned in comparisons of athletes' records. Nicasylus of Rhodes was proclaimed victor there, Tisander had victories there according to the account's context, and the Argives were said not to have kept records of Nemean victors at an earlier time.

l: statues of Olympic victors, Description of Greece
s: Statues at Olympia commemorate selected Olympic victors and related figures, including athletes, horses, kings, soldiers, and political figures. They are not a complete catalogue: some victors lacked statues, while greater renown or artistic quality could merit one. The records identify subjects, achievements, origins, patrons, artists, inscriptions, and unusual events.

l: horse-races, Description of Greece
s: Horse races begin with staggered rope releases from the starting-place so horses reach the beak together; charioteers and horses display skill and speed while facing Taraxippus-caused fear at the course outlet.

l: statue of Polydamas, Description of Greece
s: A statue of Polydamas by Lysippus stands on a lofty pedestal at Olympia; its base and inscription record Polydamas's exploits.

l: Polydamas, Description of Greece
s: Polydamas, son of Nicias and native of Scotusa, was described as the largest man of his time. Renowned for pancratium crowns and extraordinary strength, he slew lions unarmed, seized a bull, stopped a chariot, and killed three Persian Immortals at Susa after Darius attracted him with rewards. He died when a cave roof collapsed as he tried to hold up its falling rock.

l: Scotusa, Description of Greece
s: Scotusa, Polydamas's native place, was destroyed by Alexander while its people gathered in the theatre, leaving few survivors and eventual desertion.

l: people of Scotusa, Description of Greece
s: The people of Scotusa were surrounded in their theatre by Alexander, who killed men and sold women and children; survivors dwindled and left after another Macedonian reverse.

l: Alexander the king of the Pheræans, Description of Greece
s: Alexander, king of the Pheræans, seized Scotusa in peacetime, killed men gathered in its theatre, enslaved women and children, and funded mercenaries with the proceeds.

l: lions, Description of Greece
s: Lions lived in mountainous Thrace inside the river Nestus, sometimes prowled near Mount Olympus, attacked Xerxes’ army and killed grain-carrying camels; later Polydamas slew a large lion.

l: Mount Olympus, Description of Greece
s: Mount Olympus faces Macedonia, Thessaly, and Peneus; lions frequented it, where unarmed Polydamas killed a large lion.

l: Persians called Immortals, Description of Greece
s: are_persians Persians Three Persians called Immortals challenged Polydamas at Susa, and he slew all three in single combat.

l: cave, Description of Greece
s: developed crack [in its top] Polydamas entered a cave in summer with several companions. When its roof cracked and threatened to collapse, his companions fled, but Polydamas stayed and was crushed beneath the falling rock.

l: death of Polydamas, Description of Greece
s: is_a death [caused by crushing beneath a mass of rock] Polydamas's death fulfilled the warning that excessive confidence in strength could bring ruin. He was crushed to death after trying to hold up the collapsing roof of a cave while his companions escaped.

l: Euthymus, Description of Greece
s: Euthymus was a boxer from Locri near Zephyrium, reputed locally to be son of the River Cæcinus rather than Astycles. He won Olympic boxing in the 74th, 76th, and 77th Olympiads, defeated the Hero of Temesa, married the offered maiden, and reportedly lived long without dying like other men.

l: Temesa, Description of Greece
s: Temesa is an Italian town troubled by a sailor’s ghost, the Hero of Temesa, which killed inhabitants after violating a maiden. It honored him with a grove temple and annual bride until Euthymus defeated him, freeing the still-inhabited town.

l: Dorieus, Description of Greece
s: Dorieus, youngest son of Diagoras and a Rhodian pancratiast, won three successive Olympic victories and other games. After migrating to Thurii and later returning to Rhodes, he fought for Spartan interests against Athens, was captured and released by Athenians, then condemned and executed by Spartans.

l: Damagetus, Description of Greece
s: is_a pancratiast [Rhodian; winner before Dorieus] Damagetus, a son of Diagoras, won the pancratium at Olympia before his brother Dorieus surpassed him with three victories. He came to Olympia with Diagoras and Acusilaus and helped carry their father in celebration.

l: Glaucus of Carystus, Description of Greece
s: Glaucus of Carystus, originally from Anthedon and son of Demylus, was said to descend from Glaucus the sea god. A husbandman who used his hand as a ploughshare, he became a boxer, winning twice at the Pythian games and eight times each at the Nemean and Isthmian games. His son erected his boxing statue; Carystus people said he was buried on Glaucus' island.

l: statue of Euthymus, Description of Greece
s: The statue of Euthymus was made by Pythagoras and is described as especially fine. It stood near the statues of other athletes at Olympia.

l: statues of Diagoras and his family, Description of Greece
s: The statues of Diagoras and his family stood together at Olympia in an ordered group: Acusilaus, Dorieus, Damagetus, and Diagoras. The statue of Diagoras was made by Callicles, while the text also mentions the statue of Pisirodus near his maternal grandfather.

l: Hero of Temesa, Description of Greece
s: The Hero of Temesa, called Lycas, was the ghost of a sailor stoned after violating a maiden. Temesa yearly offered him its handsomest girl until Euthymus defeated him; he dived into the sea and vanished.

l: Theagenes of Thasos, Description of Greece
s: Theagenes of Thasos was an athlete, conventionally identified as Timosthenes’ son, though Thasians said Hercules, disguised as Timosthenes, was his father. Famous from boyhood for carrying off a bronze statue, he gained renowned strength and defeated Euthymus in Olympic boxing. He won at the Pythian, Nemean, Isthmian, and other contests, including a long course at Phthia, totaling 1,400 crowns. After death, statues and honors spread through Greece and among barbarians; he was reputed to cure diseases.

l: market-place of Elis, Description of Greece
s: The market-place of Elis, also called the Hippodrome, is an antique-built place of porticoes and regular streets where horses are exercised. It contains the Umpires' Hall, porticoes, altars, temples, statues, and a room where sixteen matrons weave Hera's shawl.

l: statue of Theagenes, Description of Greece
s: A statue of Theagenes, made by Glaucias the Aeginetan and located in the Altis, fell on and killed an enemy who scourged it nightly after Theagenes died. Prosecuted and cast into the sea, it was recovered by fishermen, restored by the Thasians, and sacrificed to as a god.

l: Thasian famine, Description of Greece
s: afflicts Thasos [after the statue was thrown into the sea] When the earth yielded no fruit to the Thasians, they treated the resulting dearth as a divine problem and consulted Delphi. The famine continued after they recalled some exiles, and the oracle attributed the unresolved situation to their having forgotten Theagenes.

l: worship of Theagenes, Description of Greece
s: is_practised_by Thasos [as worship of the restored statue] After the statue of Theagenes was recovered and restored, the Thasians sacrificed to it as to a god. Theagenes also received various honors from the people of Thasos and was regarded as able to cure diseases.

l: Hiero the son of Hierocles, Description of Greece
s: Hiero, son of Hierocles, was tyrant of Syracuse, rising after Agathocles’s death in the second year of the 126th Olympiad. He initially aided the Carthaginians in Sicily, then joined the Romans, befriended Pyrrhus, and was assassinated by Dinomenes; his sons dedicated Olympia statues.

l: war between Rome and Carthage for Sicily, Description of Greece
s: During the war, the Carthaginians controlled more than half of Sicily. Hiero the son of Hierocles initially joined the Carthaginians but changed sides and joined the Romans after judging Roman power to be stronger and more lasting.

l: chariot of Hiero, Description of Greece
s: A brazen chariot at Olympia, made by Onatas the Æginetan, commemorates Hiero’s Olympian victories; with horses and boys made by Calamis, it was offered to the god by Dinomenes.

l: statues of Hiero the son of Hierocles, Description of Greece
s: Two statues at Olympia, erected by Hiero’s sons and made by Mico, depict Hiero the son of Hierocles on horseback and on foot.

l: Artemidorus of Tralles, Description of Greece
s: Artemidorus of Tralles, a pancratium victor, was initially too young to win at Olympia; he later defeated boys, unbearded competitors, and leading men at Smyrna, then won Olympia among men.

l: Milo, Description of Greece
s: Milo of Croton, son of Diotimus, was a wrestling victor whose chief achievements were six Olympic prizes, including one as a boy, and six Pythian victories among men plus one as a boy. Seeking a seventh Olympic win, he lost to Timasitheus. He was associated with remarkable feats and a statue by Dameas, then died trapped in a split tree and killed by wild beasts.

l: Clitomachus of Thebes, Description of Greece
s: Clitomachus of Thebes, son of Hermocrates, was a pancratium victor and athlete. He won wrestling, boxing, and pancratium at the Isthmian games and three Pythian pancratium victories. After Olympic defeats to Theagenes, he won pancratium in the 141st Olympiad, then lost to Caprus after requesting the contest precede boxing.

l: Gorgias of Leontini, Description of Greece
s: Gorgias of Leontini, son of Carmantides, was a rhetorician said to be the first practitioner of rhetoric. Famous for eloquence at Olympia, he went with Tisias on an embassy to the Athenians, had a statue there placed by Eumolpus, and reportedly lived 105 years.

l: Anaximenes of Lampsacus, Description of Greece
s: Anaximenes of Lampsacus was a historian and sophist, noted for histories of Greece, Philip and Alexander and for early extempore oratory. Honored with a statue at Olympia, he saved Lampsacus by persuading Alexander to do the opposite of his oath, and his imitation of Theopompus incurred hostility toward Theopompus.

l: Mount Cronos, Description of Greece
s: is_behind treasuries of Olympia [extending along their length] Mount Cronos lies behind the base holding the treasuries and extends along their length. Those called the Basilæ sacrifice to Cronos on its summit at the vernal equinox in the month of Elaphius.

l: treasuries of Olympia, Description of Greece
s: are_located_on Mount Cronos [on a tufa-stone base north of Hera’s temple] The treasuries of Olympia stand on a tufa-stone base north of the temple of Hera, with Mount Cronos behind them. The unit describes treasuries belonging to the Sicyonians, Carthaginians, Epidamnus, Sybaris, Cyrene, Metapontum, Megara, and Gela, together with their dedications and inscriptions.

l: treasury of the Sicyonians, Description of Greece
s: The treasury of the Sicyonians at Olympia was an offering built by Myron after his chariot victory. It had two brass chambers, one Doric and one Ionic, and contained Myanes armour, Pelops’ gold-hilted sword, Amalthea’s ivory horn, and a boxwood Apollo with a gilt head.

l: Sosipolis, Description of Greece
s: Sosipolis is the tutelary deity of the people of Elis, honored in the inaccessible temple of Ilithyia and near Fortune. Maidens and women offer hymns and incense, without wine. In the story, a baby offered to aid the Eleans became a dragon, drove away the Arcadians, and secured an Elean victory.

l: horse-race starting-place, Description of Greece
s: The horse-race starting-place, shaped like a ship’s prow facing the course, extended more than 400 feet on each side. It assigned buildings to entrants by lot and staged the start through sequentially released ropes, a brazen dolphin, and a mechanical brazen eagle rising from an unbaked-brick altar.

l: Taraxippus, Description of Greece
s: Taraxippus is a circular altar or place at the Hippodrome’s outlet that terrifies horses, causing panic, wrecked chariots, and injured charioteers. Greeks offered several identifications; it is most plausibly identified with Poseidon Hippius.

l: battle between the Eleans and Arcadians, Description of Greece
s: In the battle between the Eleans and Arcadians, a woman offered her baby to aid Elis after a dream. The child became a dragon, frightening the Arcadians; the Eleans pursued and defeated them, and their slain were commemorated west of the Cladeus.

l: suitors of Hippodamia, Description of Greece
s: are_buried_in tomb of the suitors of Hippodamia [in a common sepulchre made by Pelops] The suitors of Hippodamia were killed by Oinomaus before Pelops defeated him. Pelops gave them a common sepulchre, and the text names many of them, including Alcathous, Euryalus, Eurymachus, Crotalus, Acrias, Capetus, Lycurgus, Lasius, Chalcodon, Tricolonus, Aristomachus, Prias, Pelagon, Aëolius, and Cronius.

l: temple of Dionysus, Description of Greece
s: has_statue_of Dionysus The temple of Dionysus is identified with the old theatre between the marketplace and the temple of the goddess Mene at Elis. Its statue of Dionysus is said to be by Praxiteles.

l: Thyia, Description of Greece
s: Thyia is a Dionysus festival celebrated by the people of Elis about eight stades from the city, where sealed empty flagons are found full of wine next day.

l: wine, Description of Greece
s: flows_spontaneously_from temple of Dionysus [annually at the feast of Dionysus on Andros] At the Thyia, three empty flagons are said to become full of wine while sealed inside a chapel. The people of Andros likewise say that wine flows spontaneously from the temple during their annual festival of Dionysus.

l: Seres, Description of Greece
s: The Seres breed Ser insects to produce garment thread, feeding them grain for four years and green reed in the fifth before collecting thread after death; traditions describe them as Ethiopian or mixed Scythian and Indian.

l: Ser, Description of Greece
s: Ser is an insect called Ser by the Greeks, about twice the largest beetle, spider-like and eight-footed. It lives in domiciles through summer and winter, spins slender thread around its feet, eats grain four years then green reed in its fifth, and dies after five years.

l: Seria, Description of Greece
s: Seria is said to be an island in the Red Sea, though another tradition says the river Ser forms it; accounts also differ over whether the Seres are Ethiopian or mixed Scythian and Indian.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: This document is a continuous section of a geographical and antiquarian description, covering Achaia, Arcadia, Bœotia, and Phocis. It combines regional origins, migrations, wars, civic change, landscapes, monuments, cults, myths, and local marvels, moving town by town along roads, rivers, mountains, and coasts. It begins in Achaia with the succession of Ægialians, Ionians, and Achæans, then follows Ionian migration to Attica and Asia Minor, including Miletus, Ephesus, Samos, Chios, and Smyrna. Achaia’s later history centers on the Achæan League: its rise, conflicts with Sparta and Macedonia, alliance with Rome, internal quarrels over Sparta and exiles, and ruin through leaders including Callicrates, Menalcidas, Diæus, and Critolaus. Roman victories by Metellus and Mummius culminate in Corinth’s destruction and Greece’s subjection. The narrative then surveys Achaean places, especially Patræ, Ægium, Helice, Ægira, and Pellene, preserving their festivals, temples, disasters, heroes, and foundations. Arcadia follows, beginning with Pelasgus, Lycaon, Arcas, and their descendants. Its account ranges through Mantinea, Orchomenus, Pheneus, Stymphelus, Clitor, Psophis, Thelpusa, Megalopolis, Lycosura, Phigalia, Pallantium, and Tegea. Major themes are Arcadian claims of great antiquity; cults of Zeus Lycæus, Despœna, Demeter, Artemis, Poseidon, and Hermes; strange waters such as the Styx and Ladon; and the rise and decline of cities. Megalopolis is founded with Theban aid after Leuctra but later devastated by Cleomenes. Philopœmen emerges as a final Greek public benefactor, fighting Spartan rulers, reforming the Achæans, resisting Roman pressure, and dying after capture in Messenia. Bœotia centers on Platæa and Thebes. Platæa’s Persian-war memory, Hera’s Dædala festival, and repeated destruction are set beside Thebes’ mythical royal history and political fortunes. Epaminondas’ victory at Leuctra, foundation of Megalopolis, restoration of Messene, and death at Mantinea mark Theban greatness, followed by Thebes’ destruction by Alexander and partial restoration. The book also explores Helicon, the Muses, Hesiod, Orpheus, Orchomenus, Trophonius’s oracle, and many sanctuaries. Phocis culminates at Delphi. After Phocian wars, the Sacred War, Macedonian intervention, and resistance to the Galati, the text describes Delphi’s oracle, temples, games, Amphictyonic Council, treasures, inscriptions, and votive offerings. It ends with Polygnotus’s paintings of Troy and Hades, then a survey of Phocian and Ozolian Locrian towns, ending at Amphissa, Myonia, Œanthea, and Naupactus.

l: Achaia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Achaia is a country and region of Greece, called Ægialus in ancient times, lying between Elis and Sicyonia on the Corinthian Gulf; the Larisus and Dyme mark its boundary with Elis. Its inhabitants gave it its name. It rose with difficulty to great eminence and became the foremost Greek power through which Rome reduced Greece. Its rulers’ folly stopped its growth: Diæus frustrated Metellus’s plan to settle it, its general meetings were suppressed, and Greece was governed by a prætor of Achaia; Augustus assigned Dyme to Patræ.

l: Elis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Elis is a Peloponnese place opposite the Echinades, bordering Messenia, the Achæans, and Heræa. Its boundary with Heræa is disputed: Arcadians name the Erymanthus, while Elis names the tomb of Corœbus. It features notable athletes and equitable umpires connected with Arrhachion's Olympia victories.

l: Sicyonia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sicyonia borders Achaia on the east. Its inhabitants attributed the ancient name Ægialus to Ægialeus, king of what was then Sicyonia.

l: Ægialus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_named_after Ægialeus [according to the tradition of the Sicyonians] Ægialus was the ancient name of the country later called Achaia. The name was said either to derive from Ægialeus or from the country's mostly seashore position, and it remained in use for a long time.

l: Ægialians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ægialians were ancient inhabitants of Ægialus, later called Ionian Ægialians after Ion, until Achæans expelled them; they are inhabitants of Achaia today.

l: Xuthus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Xuthus, exiled from Thessaly by brothers over their father's money, fled to Athens, married Erechtheus's daughter, became father of Achæus and Ion, and later lived and died in Ægialus.

l: Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Athens is a city and a recurring center of refuge, military action, worship, and political reversal. It received Xuthus after his flight from Thessaly, joined Ægialus in giving Achæus an army, invited Ion to command against the Eleusinians, and welcomed the Ionians as settlers; it later served as the starting point for the sons of Codrus and for Ionians sailing toward settlement in Asia Minor. Under Codrus it faced a night entry by Lacedæmonians, while its people also received a warning from Zeus at Dodona. Athens sheltered Platæans driven from their country and Thebans expelled by Alexander, and supported restoration of Thebes with great friendliness. It was attacked or threatened by Epaminondas, involved in the plundering of Oropus, and later held Macedonian garrisons after Demades and other traitors influenced Antipater, making Athenians slaves of the Macedonians. Its civic and sacred life included the Panathenaea, the Acropolis, three Graces, and mysteries kept from the multitude.

l: Achæus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Achæus, son of Xuthus and descendant of Hellen, took armies from Ægialus and Athens, returned to Thessaly, and recovered his ancestral throne; his sons later connected with Argos and Lacedæmon.

l: Ion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ion, son of Xuthus, married Helice, became Selinus's adopted heir, and ruled the Ægialians. He founded Helice and gave the Ægialians the additional name Ionians. Later, while commander for Athens, he died in Attica and was buried at Potamos.

l: Cecrops, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cecrops, son of Pandion and king of Athens, contemporary of Lycaon, first recognized Zeus as supreme and offered pelani instead of living sacrifices.

l: Selinus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Selinus was king of the Ægialians. He offered his only child Helice in marriage to Ion and adopted Ion as his son and heir.

l: Helice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Helice was an Achaean town and formerly important city near Ægium and the sea. Ion founded it, naming it for his wife Helice, daughter of Selinus; defeated Ionians later took refuge there. Its most important feature was the most holy temple of Poseidon of Helice, which received gifts. An earthquake and the sea overwhelmed and totally destroyed Helice; none of its people remained, Ægium occupied its territory, and its ruins became hard to find.

l: Ionians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Ionians were a people formerly called the Ægialians, a name changed after Ion ruled them. They inhabited territory later held by the Achæans, rejected the Achæans’ proposal to become colonists, fought them, endured siege at Helice, were dispossessed of territory and rule, and migrated to Attica. From Athens they formed the largest part of the expedition led by Nileus and the other sons of Codrus. They settled cities in Asia Minor, conquered Miletus, inhabited Myus and Priene, and lived or settled at Colophon, Lebedus, Teos, Erythræ, Clazomenæ, and Phocæa; at Phocæa they required kings descended from Codrus before its admission to the Pan-Ionic confederacy. They became equal fellow-citizens with Colophonian Greeks, colonized Samos, inhabited Chios, took Smyrna from the Æolians, and admitted Smyrna to the Pan-Ionic league. They possessed fertile Ionia, rich in produce and temples, and continued worship of Poseidon of Helice. Earlier, the Ionians of Aroe, Anthea, and Mesatis shared Artemis Triclaria’s temple and an all-night annual festival, but famine and sickness followed its violation until Eurypylus arrived.

l: Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Homer is a poet associated with the Iliad, the Odyssey, the Poems, and catalogues within the Iliad, especially the Catalogue of Agamemnon’s forces, the Catalogue of the ships, and the Catalogue of the Phocians. His work ranges across places, peoples, divine figures, myths, and natural features: it names Ægialus, Helice, Poseidon of Helice, Ægæ, Graia, Copæ, the palm in Delos, Great Bear, the lake Cephisis, and the tomb of Æpytus; describes Arcadians, Ilithyia, the Graces, Styx, and Achelous; and preserves such matters as the song of Linus, Sardonic laughter, and the friendship of Theseus and Pirithous. The poems distinguish what they do and do not say: the Iliad does not mention giants, while the Odyssey calls the Læstrygones giantlike and presents giants as mortal. Homer also depicts the Phæacians as near the gods, tells of the orphaned daughters of Pandareus, and represents the slaying of Otus and Ephialtes. Tradition surrounds the poet himself. He was said to have written his Poems in a cave near the springs of the Meles at Smyrna; a brazen statue of him stood at Delphi beside an oracle concerning his fatherland, death, and a riddle. Ios and Cyprus claimed him, Ios was said to contain his tomb, and Clymene or Themisto were named as his mother. Yet his fatherland and age are explicitly unknown, and blindness is associated with him. His standing is marked by the claim that the Hymns of Orpheus were second only to the Hymns of Homer in composition, while debate over his period was left unresolved.

l: Attica, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Attica was where Ion died and was buried at Potamos. It later received the Ionians as settlers when they migrated from Ægialus.

l: Dorians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Dorians were an original participating Greek state at the general Council of the Greeks. They possessed Lacedæmon when Preugenes took the statue, built a fleet at Naupactus, and, after an unsuccessful return under Hyllus, drove the Achæans from Argos and Lacedæmon. Three generations later they returned by ship near Rhium.

l: Lacedæmon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lacedæmon, also called Sparta, was a Peloponnesian region inhabited by Achæans during Agamemnon’s expedition against Ilium and before the Dorians returned. The Dorians expelled its Achæans; later the Lacedæmonians brought Tisamenus’s remains to Sparta by a Delphic oracle. It was connected by a road from Megalopolis and figured in conflicts involving Messene, the Achæans, Romans, Machanidas, Nabis, and Philopœmen. After the reverse at Leuctra, the rise of Megalopolis, and the proximity of the Messenians, it could not recover its former prosperity.

l: Argos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Argos is a town important in the days of the so-called heroes. Archander and Architeles arrived from Phthiotis, became sons-in-law of Danaus, and the population gained the Achæan name while Argives were privately called Danai. The Dorians expelled the Achæans, and Argos later lost good fortune with the overthrow of the Dorians. It has Creugas’s statue in Lycian Apollo’s temple and is reached by a road from Tegea near Hysiæ.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Achæans are a Greek people, also called Argives as a general name for the populations of Argos and Lacedæmon. Driven from Lacedæmon and Argos by the Dorians, they proposed colonization to the Ionians, defeated and expelled them, and settled in Ægialus. They inhabited twelve towns, were ruled by the sons of Tisamenus and other powerful families, and provided Greece’s largest contingent for Agamemnon’s expedition against Ilium. Later they stayed out of the fighting at Thermopylæ, the naval battles, and Platæa, allied with Athenians, fought at Chaeronea, and avoided Lamia after reverses in Boeotia. Their towns were comparatively spared tyranny, war, and plague, apart from tyranny at Pellene, and they became powerful through the Achæan League. They fought the Lacedæmonians, including at Sellasia with Antigonus, and later imposed Achæan training on them. The League had an Achæan council and a general meeting at Ægium. Philopœmen became their leading authority and repeatedly their general; the Achæans reformed their infantry under him, fought at Larisus and Mantinea, and sent Lycortas against Messenia. Their relationship with Romans became central. Though initially resentful and fearful of Roman domination, they joined Flaminius, became Roman allies, and fought Philip, the Ætolians, and Antiochus. They nevertheless resisted Roman interventions over Lacedæmonian affairs, sentenced Areus and Alcibiades to death, and were later made entirely subject to Romans through Callicrates. More than 1,000 Achæans were sent to Rome and imprisoned in Etruria. Disputes over Oropians, private embassies, and Lacedæmonians escalated. Deceived by Diæus, they raised an army, attacked Lacedæmonians at Corinth, rejected Roman decisions, and prepared war under Critolaus and Diæus. They were defeated near Scarphea and finally by Mummius, after which survivors fled from Corinth. Other episodes include honoring Œbotas before Olympia, the poverty and dispersal of Patræ after war with the Galati, the killing of suppliants at Helice before its destruction, and the capture of Phana by fouling its water supply.

l: Argives, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Argives, also called Danai, are a Peloponnesian group marked by warfare, religious offerings, athletic judgment, and later political conflict. In ancient times they introduced fire into Lerne from the shrine of Pyronian Artemis. They conducted two expeditions against Thebes, associated with Polynices and the sons of Polynices, captured Thebes, took Tiresias and spoil to Apollo at Delphi, and dedicated a brazen horse and other votive statues from victory spoils at Œnoe. In a later campaign they entered Bœotia with Arcadian and Messenian allies, initially defeated the Thebans at Ismenius, then were destroyed except for Adrastus. They honored the Epigoni and aided Epaminondas and the Thebans in restoring the Messenians. At Nemea they awarded dead Creugas victory after Damoxenus violated conditions. Finally, Gallus arbitrated their dispute with the Lacedæmonians and treated them contemptuously.

l: Tisamenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tisamenus, son of Orestes and Thersander by Demonassa, became king of the Achæans after their expulsion from Argos and Lacedæmon. Unaffected by the Furies of Laius and Oedipus, he fell fighting the Ionians, was buried at Helice, then reburied at Sparta.

l: Orestes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Orestes is described both as Agamemnon’s son and as a Roman envoy based at Corinth to settle disputes between the Lacedæmonians and Achæans. After murdering his mother Clytæmnestra, he went mad at Maniæ, damaged a finger, was healed at Ace, cut his hair, and faced pursuit by the Furies before an Areopagus trial. Following Apollo’s oracle, he migrated from Mycenæ to Arcadia; later he summoned Achæan leaders and urged restraint toward Lacedæmonian refugees.

l: Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sparta is a city marked by warfare, political dispute, civic customs, and repeated changes to its defenses and youth training. It contains the tomb of Tisamenus at Phiditia and performs funeral rites for Talthybius. During the peace of Antalcidas, Epaminondas visited on an embassy and challenged Sparta to have its neighboring towns set an example. Spartans later came to relieve the Lacedæmonians at Leuctra; Epaminondas marched against Sparta, but Agesilaus refused battle. Sparta was then associated with lost glory before Messene’s recovery. Critolaus urged the Achæans to make war on it, and Diæus said he fought for its troubles rather than against it. After defeat, survivors defended the town while nearby places received Achæan garrisons. Its gates were shut to Titus Flaminius and Diophanes; its Nabis-strengthened fortifications and walls were demolished, and Achæan training imposed. Exiles returned, walls were rebuilt, and national training was restored.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Delphi is a hilly town, also called Pytho, said to be named after Delphus. It is above all the location and source of an oracle, served by the Pythian Priestess and protected by the god according to an oracle. From the earliest notices, people and communities come or send messengers there for answers: Alcmæon, the Phigalians, Argives, Erginus, Orchomenians, Bœotians, Phocians, Homer, Themistocles, and Achæans seek guidance on madness, return, water, offspring, pestilence, danger, conquest, and other needs. Its oracle also determines names for the Athenian tribes. The town’s temple and sacred precincts are repeatedly central to conflict and defense. The Phocians seize the temple while Heraclides is President, and the temple is repeatedly plundered. Delphi later becomes a battlefield against the Galati: threatened by Brennus and the Galati, its inhabitants seek the oracle’s protection, Greek forces assemble, and the barbarians are defeated in what is called the greatest struggle between the Galati and the Greeks. Delphi is also a dense setting of temples, monuments, contests, and offerings. Four temples stand in a row at the entrance, including the temple of Athene Pronoia; nearby are the sacred enclosure of Phylacus, gymnasium, river Plistus, and spring of Castalia. Its precincts contain treasuries, statues, military and athletic memorials, the navel regarded by the Delphians as the centre of the world, inscriptions of the Seven Wise Men, and objects associated with Apollo and others. Peoples from many places send offerings, while statues of Antigonus, Demetrius, and Ptolemy arrive later. Delphi hosts the Pythian musical and athletic contests, with a theatre and a high stadium; below it, the road to the plain passes the Hippodrome for horse-races. Cirrha, its seaport, lies about 60 stades away.

l: Dorian return to the Peloponnese, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: lands_at Promontory of Rhium [by ship, rather than via the Isthmus of Corinth] During the reign of Cypselus, the Dorians returned to the Peloponnese in ships and landed near the Promontory of Rhium. This differed from their earlier attempt, led by Hyllus, which approached by way of the Isthmus of Corinth.

l: the battle between the Ionians and Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The battle began after the Ionians rejected the Achæans' proposal to become their colonists because they feared Tisamenus would rule both peoples. Tisamenus fell, the Achæans defeated the Ionians, and the Ionians fled to Helice before being allowed to leave under conditions.

l: the Ionian migration to Attica, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Ionians migrated to Attica after their conflict with the Achæans. The Athenians and their king Melanthus welcomed them, either in gratitude for Ion's service or because they feared the Dorians and valued the Ionians' strength.

l: the naming of Achaia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The country between Elis and Sicyonia was called Achaia in Pausanias's time because of its inhabitants. In earlier times it was called Ægialus, and its inhabitants were called Ægialians or, after Ion, Ionian Ægialians.

l: oracle at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The oracle at Delphi, located at Delphi and delivered by the Pythian Priestess in at least one consultation, gives warnings, commands, predictions, and guidance. It directs Eurypylus concerning a chest and a strange sacrifice; its wider prophecy ends the annual sacrifice ordered for Melanippus and Comætho when a foreign king brings a foreign god. It predicts victory connected with Codrus’s self-devotion, guides Antinoe by a serpent, warns Epaminondas about Pelagos, misunderstood as the sea rather than an oak plantation, and tells Alcmæon where vengeance cannot follow him. It also directs settlements, the removal of Arcas’s remains, mourning for Scephrus during famine, and is consulted by the people of Phigalia during famine.

l: Ægialus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ægialus is a Greek word meaning sea-shore, compared in meaning with Pomerania and Glamorganshire.

l: the sea-shore, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sea-shore is given as the meaning of the Greek word Ægialus.

l: Medon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Medon, lame in one foot, quarrels with Nileus over Athens and receives the kingdom from the Pythian Priestess.

l: Nileus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Nileus, eldest son of Codrus, refused Medon’s rule, led Ionians to Asia Minor after an oracle favored Medon, conquered Miletus, and was buried near Didymi.

l: Codrus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Codrus, son of Melanthus, was king when the Peloponnesians came to Athens. He fought for his own nation and devoted himself for Athens in accordance with the oracle at Delphi; after his death, the Peloponnesians no longer expected victory. He fathered Medon, Nileus, Androclus, and other sons, and became ancestor of leaders, settlers, and rulers connected with the Ionian cities.

l: Pythian Priestess, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Pythian Priestess is at Delphi and is an authority of Apollo’s oracle there. She issues commands and oracles to communities and individuals: she forbids the Lacedæmonians to touch Arcadia; requires funeral rites for children stoned unjustly by the people of Caphyæ; gives the Phigalians terms for returning; and directs the Orchomenians to bring Hesiod’s bones from Naupactus to cure pestilence, with a crow to reveal them. She also orders rites for Actaeon, consultation of Trophonius for drought, and military actions by the Liparæans and the ruler of Haliartus. At Delphi she proclaims Pindar’s share of firstfruits and tells Themistocles to remove Persian spoils from Apollo’s temple.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hercules is a figure presented through local traditions, monuments, temples, statues, and conflicting accounts, chiefly as the son of Amphitryon who grew up at Thebes. As a boy he killed Linus; later the Thebans say he remitted their yearly tax, mutilated envoys from Orchomenus, fought beside them against the Orchomenians, defeated Erginus, and dedicated a stone lion. They also attribute to him madness, sons by Megara, an attempted attack on Amphitryon, and works redirecting the Cephisus and blocking its passage to the sea. Expelled from Tiryns by Eurystheus, he may have lived at Pheneus with Laonome, where he dug pits and a canal for the Olbius. After capturing Elis, he was said to build the temple of Pythian Apollo; he rode Arion in war against Elis. At Eurystheus's orders he hunted the Erymanthian boar, and traditions differ on whether he killed the Stymphelian birds with arrows or drove them away with rattles. He fathered Echephron and Promachus by Psophis, and a Phigalian story has him rescue Phialo and her exposed boy. He received Dexamenus's hospitality, loved Sostratus and erected his tomb, and is associated with a cave and small statue at the Buraicus. After killing Iphitus, he fought Apollo over and carried off a tripod before returning it. Accounts also distinguish him from Egyptian Hercules, question whether he founded an ancient temple, and identify another Hercules as an Idæan Dactyli.

l: Miletus (the Cretan leader), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Miletus, a Cretan leader, fled Minos with a force, led Cretans to Anactoria, and gave his name to the renamed town and country of Miletus.

l: Coresus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Coresus, a Calydonian priest of Dionysus, grievously loves Callirhoe despite her dislike; when Dionysus afflicts the Calydonians, he sacrifices himself instead of her.

l: Pindar, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
