s: Pindar was a poem-writer who composed in Doric, visited Thespiæ when young, and was said to begin writing after bees left honey on his lips. Though defeated by Corinna at Thebes, reportedly because she used Aeolic, he became famous throughout Greece. The Pythian Priestess at Delphi granted him firstfruits with Apollo; he also dedicated a statue of Hermes Agoræus and sent a Hymn honoring Ammon. In old age Proserpine appeared in his dream; he died before its tenth day, and afterward a related woman recorded his Hymn to Proserpine from a dream.

l: Theseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Theseus is associated with the Panathenaea, which acquired its name in his time. Returning from Crete, he instituted games to Apollo at Delos and began crowning victors with palm, establishing palm as a prize of victory. His famous friendship with Pirithous ends with both seated on an enchanted rock that grew to them instead of fetters, while Theseus holds both swords.

l: Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Dionysus is a god worshipped through temples, statues, festivals, titles, prayers, and oracles. His presence is carried between places: a statue brought from Calydon is worshipped at Patræ as Calydonian, and a statue in a chest received after the capture of Ilium reaches Aroe, where its arrival is linked to the end of human sacrifice to Artemis Triclaria and to an annual festival. At Calydon he answers his priest Coresus by afflicting the Calydonians with insanity and death; an oracle declares the suffering his wrath. He can also free and empower captives, as Lysian Dionysus does for Thebans, and he aids the women of Tanagra against Triton, defeating him. His worship includes winter sacrifice at Cynætha and processions of named statues at Patræ. Statues and temples mark him at many sites, including works by Euclides, Lysippus, and Myro. He is angry with Antiope after Dirce’s death, gives an oracle concerning Libethra, takes Ariadne from Theseus, and is said to be the first to invade India and build a bridge over the Euphrates.

l: Androclus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Androclus, son of Codrus, was appointed king of the Ionians who sailed to Ephesus. He drove Leleges and Lydians from its upper part, took Samos from the Samians, later helped Priene against the Carians, and died in that battle; his tomb lay on the road to the Magnesian gates.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Athenians are the people of Athens, portrayed through their wars, alliances, religious practices, benefactions, and eventual hardship. Early records place them in an Ionian expedition, disputes over kingship, colonization, and traditions connected with their Acropolis. They are repeatedly associated with naval strength: they possess and use triremes, evacuate Greeks from Thermopylæ by sea, fight under Themistocles off Eubœa and at Salamis, and later attack the Galati from ships. Their renowned actions win Greece's goodwill, and their ancient renown gives them command of the allied Greeks; they show exceptional valour at Thermopylæ and against the Galati. Their successes include fighting with the Platæans at Marathon and against Mardonius, defeating Thebans in border fighting, and victories at the Eurymedon. They commemorate victories with treasuries, spoils, shields, statues, a bronze palm, and offerings to Athene, Theseus, and Poseidon. They guard the temple at Delos, preserve the offerings in the temple of Olympian Zeus after taking it at Syracuse, honour Auxo and Hegemone, and pray to the Graces. They also shelter or restore others: they receive the Platæans after expulsions, allow Lacedæmonian suppliants to depart safely, aid the restoration of Thebes, and help restore Phocian towns. The account also stresses reversals and errors. They suffer defeat at Delium, a reverse at Aegospotami, survive the Peloponnesian War and plague, and undertake a fatal war against Syracuse after misreading an oracle. After Macedonian power subdues them, raids and weak allies lead them to depend on Rome. Reduced to extreme poverty, they plunder Oropus, leave a fine unpaid, resist Oropian demands, and plunder it again. Thus celebrated naval courage and public dedications give way to defeat, dependence, and poverty.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Greeks are a broad collective appearing across shared religious practice, warfare, settlement, memory, and representation. In early times they honored unhewn stones as gods. Before sailing from Aulis, they consulted Calchas about sacrificing Iphigenia; adverse winds detained them until Artemis substituted a doe, after which favorable winds came. After the capture of Ilium, they shared spoil including a chest with a statue of Dionysus, prepared to sail, and administered an oath to Ajax over Cassandra’s violation; they also spared Laodice out of regard for Antenor’s family. They commemorate common struggles through joint tombs, trophies, and dedications. Those killed against the Medes had a common tomb near Platæa, and after that battle the Greeks jointly offered a golden tripod. Greeks who fought the Persian King dedicated a brazen Zeus at Olympia and an Apollo at Delphi after Artemisium and Salamis. They later suffered a fatal defeat at Chæronea, while Epaminondas was credited with winning their freedom. Their unity is repeatedly tested. They were initially not banded together, enabling the Achæans to grow powerful, while Philip established garrisons and raided Greek communities; Flaminius sought the Achæans as Roman allies and Philip was required to remove seized garrisons. In the invasion by the Galati, Greeks defended Thermopylæ, fought and buried their dead and Galatian dead, were evacuated when threatened with encirclement, then assembled at Delphi and defeated the retreating enemy. The records also show Greeks as settlers and traders: Cretans under Rhacius reached Claros, Greeks helped found several communities, and they came to Sardinia under Aristaeus, where later conflict nearly destroyed them. They preserve prophetic traditions, including Herophile, and are portrayed collectively through named figures in scenes after Ilium.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Thebans are a people of Thebes, associated with Cadmea and with civic traditions, sanctuaries, monuments, sacrifices, and burial places. They maintain accounts of Cadmus’s settlement, altered their sacrifice to Apollo Spodius from bulls to working oxen, and honor figures including Pronomus, Epaminondas, Iolaus, Zethus, and Amphion. Their earlier traditions include defeat and tribute after killing Clymenus, remission through Hercules, conflict with Orchomenians, flight after Glisas, settlement at Homole, and restoration to Thebes by Thersander. Their political and military story centers on changing alliances, severe reversals, and repeated recovery. They were first friendly with the Lacedæmonians, later joined the Corinthians against them, captured Platæa, fought Athenians with both defeats and victory at Delium, and faced wars involving Orchomenians, Phocians, and Peloponnesians. Epaminondas is credited with raising them from obedience to other Greek states into a foremost power. Their decisive victory at Leuctra, fought for their country, wives, and children, enabled them to expel Lacedæmonian Harmosts and decemvirates; they also aided Arcadian colonization and the founding of Megalopolis. Yet they fought the Phocians for ten years with mixed success, suffered most heavily among the Greeks at Chæronea, and buried those who fell against Philip in a common sepulchre. After Philip’s death they ejected the Macedonian garrison, but Alexander expelled them from Thebes. Survivors escaped chiefly to Athens, while some reached Acræphnium; Cassander later restored them with allies, and they rebuilt their walls. In later affairs they joined Mithridates against Rome under Pytheas, were punished for earlier actions against several peoples, and afterward sought Roman friendship. Although Roman favor eventually restored territory taken after Sulla’s invasion of Bœotia, the lower city was largely deserted in the narrator’s time.

l: Minyæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Minyæ, subjects of Minyas, took their name from him and remained distinct under Orchomenus. After Hercules remitted the yearly tax, they suffered reverses against Thebans, then were led to Troy by Ascalaphus and Ialmenus.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Lacedæmonians are a Greek people of Sparta, repeatedly defined by war, shifting alliances, internal upheaval, and eventual subordination within the Achæan League. They fought widely: they besieged and captured Platæa, invaded Tegea, Arcadia, Phigalia, Mantinea, and Megalopolis, and at times defeated opponents or captured their cities. They also suffered major reverses, including defeat at Tegea, defeat and heavy losses at Leuctra, where Epaminondas kept them shut up before permitting their departure, and later weakening by the Achæans. Their power had first been reduced by Epaminondas and afterwards through war with the Achæans; after Leuctra, their decemvirates and Harmosts were removed from towns liberated by the Thebans. Their relations with neighboring peoples repeatedly changed: Arcadians once served with them but later joined the Thebans; Mantinea was alternately conquered, allied, and hostile; and they were uniquely described as Greeks openly unfriendly to the Achæans. Under Cleomenes they changed from the Spartan kingdom, fought the Achæans and Antigonus at Sellasia, and later captured Megalopolis. Under Philopœmen, their light troops won at Mantinea but their hoplites were routed; he subsequently forced them into the Achæan League. Their impending civil war brought the exile of about 300 leaders and the sale of about 3,000 Helots. After Nabis was overthrown, they became their own masters but were brought into the League. Achæan measures destroyed Sparta’s fortifications and replaced their youth training, while the Romans later restored their national training. Disputes over jurisdiction, land, exiles, fines, and alleged Roman decisions led them to appeal to Metellus and the Roman Senate, send embassies, and seek relief while acknowledging they could not fight the Achæans. They nevertheless took up arms, were defeated with about 1,000 losses, and later violated a truce to sack Iasus. The records also preserve their killing of suppliants at Tænarum, followed by a violent earthquake, alongside an episode in which Athenian protection allowed Lacedæmonian suppliants to depart safely.

l: Phocians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Phocians are a Greek people, inhabitants of Phocis, whose record centers on war, Delphi, punishment for sacrilege, and restoration through later fighting. They participated in the war against Ilium and were constant enemies of the Thessalians. Before the Persian invasion, they defeated the Thessalians through stratagems including buried earthenware pots against cavalry and a night attack; after losing Gelon and 300 picked men, they prepared to destroy their own women, children, and possessions rather than yield, but won under their commanders and Tellias of Elis. From the spoils they offered or dedicated works to Apollo, Athene, Artemis, and a group of Hercules and Apollo fighting for a tripod at Delphi. When the Persians entered Europe, they were reportedly compelled to join Xerxes, but deserted the Medes and fought for the Greeks at Platæa. Afterward, an Amphictyonic fine was imposed on them. They then seized the temple at Delphi, employed mercenaries, and fought the Thebans for ten years. Defeat near Neon ended this course: their commanders died or were deposed, they lost participation in the temple and the general Greek Council, and their Amphictyonic votes went to the Macedonians. They returned from villages to Phocian towns, except those always weak, and their towns were later rebuilt with Athenian and Theban help. They subsequently fought at Chæronea and against Antipater and the Macedonians at Lamia and Crannon. Their decisive renewal came when Brennus and the Galati attacked Delphi. They bravely defended Thermopylæ but were overpowered; then men from every town defended Delphi, used their knowledge of Parnassus to attack the Celtic rear, guarded cattle, and endured heavy losses. Fighting the Galati and Celtic army more bravely than any other Greeks, they avenged the god at Delphi and, in the author’s view, atoned for the impiety of the other towns. They were restored to the Amphictyonic Council and their former position.

l: Cretans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cretans, a Greek group, came under Miletus to the country near Miletus when it was called Anactoria and were admitted by earlier-settled Carians to share the territory. Later, they are said to have been the first Greeks at Claros, arriving powerfully under Rhacius, attacking and capturing Apollo’s colonists.

l: Carians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Carians were a group settled near Miletus before the Cretans, sharing the country with them and holding much of the land around Claros when the first Greeks arrived. They mixed with Greeks at Teos and Erythræ, but were driven from several cities and from Colophon’s territory.

l: the sons of Codrus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The sons of Codrus disputed or received leadership after Medon’s assignment, then founded colonies: Nileus and others departed, Androclus led Ionians to Ephesus, and Cyaretus colonized Myus.

l: Sardinia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sardinia is a large, fertile island, also called Ichnusa by Greeks engaged in commerce and named after Sardus. It is 1,120 stades long and 470 broad. It received settlers and colonists including Libyans, Greeks, Iberes, Thespians, Athenians, and Trojans, and contains Nora, Olbia, Ogryle, Caralis, and Sulci. Its northern range toward Italy lacks harbours and sends violent winds over the sea; central air is pestilential. It lacks serpents and wolves, but has swift rams and deadly grass near springs.

l: Orchomenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Orchomenus is a Greek city and kingdom of the Minyae, beyond Laphystium. It is approached from Mantinea by two roads: one through Ladas’ course and several named sights, and another by Mount Anchisia along the boundary with Mantinea. Its old town stood on a hilltop, with ruined walls and marketplace; the later town lay inside the old circuit. Its territory includes a small marshy plain, routes toward Caphya, Stymphelus, and Pheneus, and connections to Caphyæ by a ravine road and a road beside the lake; its water is stored in a reservoir in Caphyæ’s plain. The city’s notable places include a well, temples of Poseidon, Aphrodite, Dionysus, and the ancient Graces, a cedar-tree image of Artemis, sacred meteoric stones, stone statues, the treasury and tomb of Minyas, and the tomb of Hesiod. Its people annually honor Actaeon and recovered Hesiod’s bones from Naupactus after consulting Delphi. Its history begins with Andreus as first inhabitant. Once famous, renowned, prosperous, and wealthy even during the Trojan War, it later faced an end likened to Mycenæ and Delos. After the posterity of Almus ended childless, the kingdom passed to Clymenus; its power declined through the deity, and Philip son of Amyntas restored it to the Orchomenians after the Thebans had driven them out. In the narrator’s day it had only moderate wealth.

l: Asia Minor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Asia Minor is a place reached by people sent by Apollo, where the sons of Codrus and other Greek groups colonized maritime towns and established cities including Miletus, Ephesus, Priene, and Myus.

l: Miletus (city), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Miletus, an Ionian city, was called Anactoria for two generations under Anax and Asterius before Nileus and the Ionians conquered it, killing men and marrying women.

l: Crete, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Crete is a place marked by civil war during Philopœmen’s service, competing traditions about Cydon, Catreus, and Gortys, and associations with Dædalus at Minos’ court and the work of Chirisophus. Tegeans describe migrants naming Cydonia and Gortys; Cretans give different parentage.

l: Ephesus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ephesus is a place associated with Ephesus, thought to be son of the river Cayster. Before the Ionian settlement, Leleges and Lydians inhabited it; Androclus expelled those in the upper city while temple-district inhabitants stayed peaceful. Later it received Colophon and Lebedus colonists, who resisted Lysimachus and Macedonians.

l: Samos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: An island near Mycale, Samos was inhabited by reluctantly received Ionian colonists; expelled Samians settled elsewhere, then recovered it from Ephesians, with Leogorus recovering it ten years later.

l: Priene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_an_ionian_city Ionian city [colonized by Thebans and Ionians mixed] Priene was colonized by Thebans and Ionians under Philotas and Æpytus, and the Carians were driven from it. It was later ravaged by Tabalus the Persian and by Hiero, one of its own citizens, before becoming an Ionian city.

l: Myus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Myus was colonized by Cyaretus, son of Codrus, after Ionians drove out Carians. Its inhabitants later left for Miletus when the bay became a mosquito-filled marsh, taking possessions and divine statues. In the narrator’s time, only a white-marble temple of Dionysus remained.

l: expedition of the Ionians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The expedition of the Ionians was led by Nileus and the other sons of Codrus and included people from Athens, Thebes, Orchomenus, Phocis, and Eubœa. After reaching Asia Minor, its detachments went to different maritime towns, including Miletus, Ephesus, Priene, and Myus.

l: Ionian migration, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Ionian migration brought the sons of Codrus and various Greek peoples to Asia Minor. The settlers conquered or occupied coastal cities and were not all related to the Ionians by race, since the sons of Codrus were Messenian through their fathers' ancestry and Athenian through their mother's side.

l: conquest of Miletus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: During the conquest of Miletus, the Ionians killed all the male inhabitants except those who escaped from the captured city. They married the surviving women and daughters.

l: marsh formation at Myus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Mæander filled the bay mouth near Myus with mud, creating a mosquito-breeding marsh whose foul stagnant water drove Myus inhabitants to Miletus.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Apollo is a god whose identity is expressed through worship, oracles, protection, conflict, love stories, and many temples, statues, and offerings. He is associated with oxen, appears in forms ranging from old wooden and cedarwood images to a square Hermæ, seated figures, bronze works, and a gold statue, and bears names including Pythian Apollo, Apollo the Helper, Averter of Ill, Ismenius, and Sitalcas. He receives Manto and other captives at Delphi, sends them toward Asia Minor and Claros, and directs Manto to Ionia. His central importance is the Delphic oracle: Earth gave its share to Themis, Themis gave it to Apollo, and Apollo gave Poseidon a share in exchange for Calauria near Troezen. He gives oracles and divinatory power, protects the Delphians, and is honored through contests, hymns, laurel crowns, sacrifices, statues, tithes, sayings, and votive offerings. Apollo acts forcefully: he slays the dragon, Caanthus, Otus, Ephialtes, and Linus; is shown shooting at Tityus; and fights Hercules for a tripod. He aids communities in pestilence, especially the Phigalians and Athenians, and receives offerings after victories and deliverances. His loves include Bolina, who escapes into the sea, Daphne, and Acacallis; his love for Daphne is linked to jealousy of Leucippus and to the laurel crown. Temples, sanctuaries, sacred places, and oracles devoted to him endure across the records, though Delphi is repeatedly plundered and its statues removed. The account closes with his hippodrome near Delphi, Pythian horse-races, and the consequences of impiety against his sacred territory.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Artemis is a goddess whose presence is chiefly expressed through widespread worship, temples, statues, festivals, sacrifices, and accounts of her power. From the outset she is associated with the temple of Ephesian Artemis, whose worship predates the Ionian migration; Amazons had sacrificed and sought refuge there, while Coresus and Ephesus are said to have built it. This sanctuary is described as the finest in Ionia for size and opulence. She appears in forms and titles including the Huntress, Hymnia, Hemerasia, the Leader, Hegemone, Triclaria, and The Most Beautiful, and is represented as a huntress and archer. Her sanctuaries extend across many places: at Ægira, Stymphelus, Lusi, Tegea, Hyampolis, Bulis, near Acacesium, and on hills and rocks. Arcadians worshipped Artemis Hymnia throughout Arcadia; rules governing her priesthood changed after a priestess was defiled at her altar. Neglect or improper observance of her rites brings severe consequences: at Stymphelus, a negligently celebrated festival was followed by a blocked river and flooding; Artemis Triclaria’s anger after her temple was violated was said to bring famine, sickness, and unusual mortality. Her annual human sacrifice, ordered by an oracle, continued until Eurypylus brought a chest containing the statue of Dionysus, ending it. Artemis acts decisively in legend and ritual. She kills Buphagus for attempting her chastity, shoots Limon in vengeance for Scephrus, punishes people who neglect Leto, and is depicted shooting at Tityus. She shoots Callisto when Callisto is a she-bear, gives Procris a dog, and causes a doe to be sacrificed at Aulis instead of Iphigenia. She inspires a stratagem against the Sicyonians, stirs Chronius in a dream against Aristomelidas, and helps appease Apollo during his anger over the tripod. Her images emphasize hunting and light: deer skin, quiver, hunting dog, torches or lamp, and two dragons. The records end with temples and statues where she holds a torch and is accompanied by a dog, reaffirming her continuing cult presence.

l: temple of Apollo at Claros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Apollo at Claros is a temple the Colophonians regard as most ancient.

l: oracle of Apollo at Claros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: An oracle at Claros, regarded by the Colophonians as most ancient.

l: Claros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Claros, containing an oracle and an unfinished temple of Apollo, was reached by Cretans and captives; after conflict before Rhacius, it later received Smyrna’s envoys seeking the oracle.

l: Rhacius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Rhacius, a Cretan leader, leads Cretans to Claros, then understands Manto’s identity and mission, marries her, and makes her companions fellow-settlers.

l: Thersander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Thersander, Polynices' son, leads Epigoni to take Thebes, then Telephus kills him sailing toward Troy; his tomb is at Elaea.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Thebes is a city and town in Bœotia, bounded from the district of Platæa by the Asopus and approached by roads from Platæa, Potniæ, and Chalcis. First inhabited by the Ectenes under Ogygus, it was repeopled by the Hyantes and Aones after the Ectenes died out. Cadmus established Cadmea; Amphion and Zethus joined the lower town to it, named the city for Thebe, and gave it seven-gated walls. Cadmea later became its citadel. Its history is marked by repeated conflict, power, and decline. It faced attacks by Erginus, Argives, and the Epigoni, and endured dynastic conflict. It was formerly at the head of Greece and secured Greece's freedom and autonomy through its arms, but was governed by an oligarchy during the Persian invasion. After Chæronea, Philip placed a garrison there; after his death it was expelled, and warnings of ruin followed. Alexander attacked and laid Thebes waste, while Cassander later restored it and rebuilt its old walls. It nevertheless grew progressively weaker. In the Roman advance, after joining the Achæans in war, its inhabitants abandoned it; Pytheas was captured and executed, while Metellus spared its temples, buildings, and fugitives. Thebes preserves a dense landscape of gates, temples, monuments, statues, tombs, and traditions: Cadmus's settlement site, sanctuaries of Dionysus, Demeter, Ammon, Fortune, Aphrodite, and Hercules, tombs of Menœceus and Melanippus, sites tied to Oedipus, Antigone, Amphion, Semele, and others, and annual rites and funeral sacrifices. In the author's day its lower part was deserted except for temples, and only the citadel and a few inhabitants remained; the inhabited citadel was then called Thebes rather than Cadmea.

l: Manto, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Manto, daughter of Tiresias, is captured after Thebes falls and taken to Apollo at Delphi. Sent to Asia Minor to found a colony, she reaches Claros in Colophonia, explains the captives' purpose to Rhacius, marries him, and becomes Mopsus's parent.

l: Tiresias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tiresias is a prophet, encountered by Odysseus in Hades for counsel about returning home. He beheads a serpent with his sword. Taken by Argives and Polynices’ sons toward Apollo at Delphi, he drinks at Tilphusa, dies, and is buried there; Thebans nevertheless display a cenotaph, admitting he died in Haliartia.

l: Haliartus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Haliartus is a city that supported the Greeks during the invasion of the Medes and was attacked by part of Xerxes' army. It contains the tomb of Lysander, who fell when forces from Thebes and Athens sallied out, as well as a hero-chapel, temples, and the river Lophis in its district.

l: Mopsus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: expels Carians [altogether from the country] Mopsus, the son of Rhacius and Manto, drove out all the Carians altogether.

l: Colophonian Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_as_fellow_citizens Ionians [on equal terms] The Colophonian Greeks became fellow-citizens on equal terms with the Ionians. They were the only colonists at Ephesus who fought against Lysimachus and the Macedonians.

l: Colophon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Colophon, associated with Cretan, Ionian, and other Greek settlement after Mopsus drove out the Carians, had colonists at Ephesus who alone fought Lysimachus and the Macedonians. Lysimachus later dispeopled it; its fallen lay in tombs on the road to Claros.

l: Lysimachus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lysimachus dispeopled Colophon and Lebedus in order to increase the population of Ephesus. The colonists of Colophon fought against him and the Macedonians at Ephesus.

l: Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Macedonians are a people associated with Pieria and Dium, where they offer Apollo a doe and, unlike others, do not customarily erect trophies after victories. They say Orpheus was slain in Pieria and removed his remains from destroyed Libethra to Dium. Hostility between Arcadians and Lacedæmonians increased their power under Philip, son of Amyntas. They gained Amphictyonic standing after the Sacred War, receiving the Phocians’ votes and later supplying six council members. They fought at Chæronea and later faced an Athenian war. Under Antigonus as regent and then Philip, son of Demetrius, they held garrisons at Corinth, Chalcis, Magnesia, and Elatea. Their supremacy was fatally damaged by decisive defeat to Flaminius and the Romans at Cynoscephalæ, forcing withdrawal from Greek towns. Under Perseus they were again defeated by Romans after his attack on Abrupolis and the Sapæans; they also held Athenians in slavery after Lamia.

l: Smyrna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Smyrna is a city, first one of the twelve Æolian cities at the old city. Taken by Ionians from Colophon, it was admitted to the Pan-Ionic league. After an oracle at Claros approved, its inhabitants moved to the modern city on Mount Pagus. It especially worships two Nemeses, has a temple of Æsculapius, and practises divination by omens.

l: Lebedus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lebedus, originally inhabited by Carians, was taken by Andræmon and Ionians, noted for numerous agreeable warm sea baths, then dispeopled by Lysimachus to enlarge Ephesus.

l: Teos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Teos, a place, was colonized by Minyæ from Orchomenus with Athamas; Carians mixed with Greeks, then Ionians led by Apœcus and settlers from Attica and Bœotia were received.

l: Athamas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Athamas lived in Athamantium, was associated with Laphystian Zeus, and received land near Laphystium from Andreus. Believing no male children survived, he adopted Haliartus and Coronus; after Phrixus or Presbon returned, Thersander’s sons yielded his kingdom to Phrixus and descendants.

l: Apœcus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a descendant of Melanthus [great-great-grandson] Apœcus, a great-great-grandson of Melanthus, led the Ionians to Teos. He and the people of Teos hospitably received later settlers from Attica and Bœotia.

l: Bœotia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Bœotia is a region contiguous to Attica, said to be named for Bœotus, son of Itonus and the Nymph Melanippe. It contains various towns and places, including Thebes, Lebadea, Leuctra, Teumessus, Glisas, Harma, Mycalessus, Aulis, Alalcomenæ, Anthedon, Mount Messapium, and the Euripus. Its communities joined the festival of Dædala, and its oaks near Alalcomenæ were noted for fine roots. It was a setting for the Argive host and the battle at Ismenius, for conflict involving Thebans and other Bœotians, and for Epaminondas’s return with the Thebans. Telchinians migrated there and may have built a temple of Athene Telchinia. It also contains works of Dædalus at Thebes and Lebadea.

l: Erythræi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Erythræi say they came from Crete with Erythrus, who founded their city; later Lycians, Carians, Pamphylians, and Greeks lived there.
